title: Scrub turkey

names.note: The dictionary separates it from wungku 'domestic turkey, not the scrub turkey'.

identification.basis: The dictionary glosses diwan as 'scrub turkey'. Queensland Parks and Wildlife Service gives diwan for the Australian brush-turkey on Eastern Kuku Yalanji country. Roth's 1901 Cape Bedford word list gives the same word, de-wan, for 'scrub-turkey (Talegalla Lathami)', an old name for this bird.

summary: **[Diwan](word:diwan)**, the scrub turkey or Australian brush-turkey (*Alectura lathami*), is the big black mound-building bird of the rainforest. It has a bare red head and a yellow wattle [ref:qld-brushturkey]. Kuku Yalanji knowledge ties it to the seasons. The dictionary records that diwan normally lives in the high country but comes down to feed when **[junjun](word:junjun)** fruit ripens in March–May. It also names a mountain locust, **[kalkamal](word:kalkamal)**, 'which tells when to collect turkey eggs' [ref:hershberger1982]. The male builds a huge compost mound and the females bury their eggs in it, up to 24 of them about half a metre down [ref:qld-brushturkey]. Nearby rainforest peoples caught the birds in [lawyer-cane](entry:lawyer-cane) traps along their daily paths [ref:roth1901].

sections.heading: Names
sections.body: The dictionary gives **[diwan](word:diwan)** 'scrub turkey'. It is careful to keep it apart from *[wungku](word:wungku)* 'domestic turkey, not the scrub turkey', the introduced farm bird, and from *[kurrbal](word:kurrbal)* 'plain turkey (native companion)', a bird of the open plains [ref:hershberger1982]. The word is shared with Kuku Yalanji's northern neighbours. Roth's 1901 Cape Bedford (Guugu Yimithirr) list gives *de-wan* for the scrub-turkey [ref:roth1901-b2].

sections.heading: Description
sections.body:
A large ground bird, 60–75 cm long, with blue-black feathers, an upright, flattened tail held like a fan, and a bare, featherless red head and neck. The male has a bright yellow wattle at the base of the neck. The female's wattle is smaller and paler [ref:qld-brushturkey]. It feeds by raking leaf litter and tearing open rotten logs with its big feet, looking for insects, seeds and fallen fruit [ref:am-brushturkey].

The male builds a **mound** of plant litter and soil, usually 2–4 m across and about 1 m high. He adds or removes material to keep the inside at a steady 33 °C [ref:qld-brushturkey]. The heat of the mound, not the parent's body, hatches the eggs. The chicks hatch after about 50 days and are independent straight away [ref:qld-brushturkey].

sections.heading: Where it lives
sections.body: The brush-turkey ranges along eastern Australia from Cape York Peninsula to the Sydney region. It lives in rainforest and wet forest and also in drier scrubs, and northern birds move to higher altitudes in winter [ref:am-brushturkey]. That matches the Kuku Yalanji record that diwan normally lives in the high country and comes down at junjun time [ref:hershberger1982].

sections.heading: Seasons
sections.body:
Kuku Yalanji reads the turkey's year from other living things [ref:hershberger1982]:

- **[Junjun](word:junjun)** is a wild fruit 'ripe in March – May'. 'During the junjun season, the scrub turkey, which normally lives in the high country, will come down to feed on them' [ref:hershberger1982]. This is the time to hunt the bird itself.
- **[Kalkamal](word:kalkamal)** is 'a locust in the mountains which tells when to collect turkey eggs'. The same word also names 'the time to collect the eggs' [ref:hershberger1982].

Zoologists record that brush-turkeys can breed at any time of year, with a peak from September to December [ref:qld-brushturkey]. That peak is the time when the mounds hold the most eggs.

sections.heading: Uses
sections.body:
**Meat and eggs.** Both were food. The dictionary links diwan to hunting the bird (junjun season) and to collecting its eggs (kalkamal) [ref:hershberger1982]. Kuku Yalanji has words for every part of an egg: *[diburr](word:diburr)* 'egg', *[yijirr](word:yijirr)* 'shell of egg', *[birukay](word:birukay)* 'yolk of the egg' and *[jamal](word:jamal)* 'white of egg' [ref:hershberger1982]. One mound can hold eggs from several females, up to 24 in all, laid into holes about half a metre deep and covered over [ref:qld-brushturkey]. That made a single well-tended mound a rich, reusable store of food.

Speaking of North Queensland generally, Roth wrote that birds', [crocodile](entry:saltwater-crocodile) and [turtle](entry:sea-turtle) eggs were taken 'whenever found' [ref:roth1901].

sections.heading: How it was caught, gathered and cooked
sections.body:
**Trapping the bird.** No published account describes turkey trapping on the Bloomfield itself. The fullest record comes from the rainforest people of the **Russell River**, south of Cairns [ref:roth1901]:

1. **Find the path.** A scrub turkey 'usually pass[es] along the same path daily' to and from water. Pick the exact spot on it.
2. **Build the trap** from **[lawyer cane](entry:lawyer-cane)**. Stick a row of cane hoops into the ground and join them with cane strips along the top and sides. An average trap is about 4 ft long, about 1½ ft high near the entrance, and about 15 in wide at the mouth.
3. **Bait it** well in the morning with nuts and fruit.
4. **About sundown, hide** in a shelter of leafy branches about 12 ft away, directly in front of the opening.
5. **Rush out** the moment the turkey walks into the trap. A hunter usually built **two traps** close together so he could work both from one hide.

On the **Tully River** the same kind of trap had 'wings' of brush or half-hoops of cane to steer the bird in, and took about half a day to set up. The hunter crouched behind the wings under a cover of leaves and **called** the turkey in [ref:roth1901].

**Gathering the eggs.** The sources give the timing (the *[kalkamal](word:kalkamal)* locust) [ref:hershberger1982] and the biology, but no published step-by-step Kuku Yalanji account of opening a mound has been found. The eggs lie in holes about half a metre deep in the mound, and each hole is covered over after laying [ref:qld-brushturkey]. Collecting means digging down into the warm litter by hand to reach them.

**Cooking.** Roth describes two ways of cooking meat [ref:roth1901]:

1. **Roast** it on and in the hot ashes, the simplest way (*[dindal](word:dindal)* 'to roast on coals') [ref:hershberger1982].
2. Or **bake** it in the Bloomfield stone **[earth oven](entry:earth-oven)** (*[kurrma](word:kurrma)*). Heat the stones, dig the hole where the fire was, line it with [ginger](entry:wild-ginger) leaves, pack in the meat with the hot stones and ashes, then cover with leaves or [tea-tree bark](entry:paperbark) and a layer of earth [ref:roth1901] [ref:hershberger1982].

sections.heading: Safety
sections.body: Brush-turkeys are not dangerous to people. The cautions are practical ones. A mound is used through a long laying season and each egg takes about 50 days to hatch [ref:qld-brushturkey], so eggs dug from one mound can be at very different stages of development. Only a small share of eggs ever become adult birds, as few as one in 200 [ref:qld-brushturkey], so the mounds matter to the bird's future. Cook meat and eggs through.

sections.heading: On Country today
sections.body:
The Australian brush-turkey is listed as Least Concern under Queensland's *Nature Conservation Act 1992* [ref:qld-brushturkey]. Like other native animals it is still protected, and anyone else needs a licence or permit to take it or its eggs [ref:qld-nca].

Section 211 of the *Native Title Act 1993* protects native title holders hunting and gathering for **personal, domestic or non-commercial communal needs** [ref:alrc-s211]. Each place below says whose country it is. Visitors must ask the Traditional Owners first.

sections.heading: Language
sections.body: Words around the turkey: *[diwan](word:diwan)* 'scrub turkey'; *[junjun](word:junjun)*, the wild fruit that brings it down from the hills; *[kalkamal](word:kalkamal)*, the locust that signals egg time; *[diburr](word:diburr)* 'egg'; *[yijirr](word:yijirr)* 'shell of egg'; *[birukay](word:birukay)* 'yolk'; *[jamal](word:jamal)* 'white of egg'; *[minya](word:minya)* 'meat, eggs (protein food)'; *[wungku](word:wungku)* 'domestic turkey' [ref:hershberger1982].

locations.summary: Brush-turkeys live in the Hann country. The Atlas of Living Australia holds 148 brush-turkey records, from 1976 to 2025, in a box of about 90 × 85 km around the middle Hann, Laura and western Rinyirru, most of them from birdwatchers' lists; it also holds 9 records of the smaller orange-footed [scrub hen](entry:scrub-hen), 2014–2023 [ref:ala-hann]. No published record from the Hann's own peoples speaks of the brush-turkey.

sections.heading: Which turkey
sections.body:
- **Brush-turkey** (this page): black, with a bare red head, in the thick scrub [ref:qld-brushturkey]. In the Atlas, 44 of the records from around the Hann are labelled with the Cape York subspecies *purpureicollis* [ref:ala-hann], the form of 'the northern Cape York Peninsula', 'smaller than the more widespread nominate subspecies' and with a purple wattle rather than a yellow one [ref:wiki-brushturkey]. Which form lives on the Hann, the record does not settle.
- **The 'plain turkey'** of the open grassland is a different bird, the [bustard](entry:bustard), which can be seen in Rinyirru's grasslands [ref:qpws-rinyirru-culture]. The Court recorded a Possum man's evidence of 'hunting pigs, kangaroos, goanna, porcupine, and plain turkeys' [ref:fca-possum]: keep the two turkeys apart.
- **[Scrub hen](entry:scrub-hen)** (orange-footed scrubfowl): smaller, brown, with orange legs; recorded in the same box [ref:ala-hann].

sections.heading: Where it lives here
sections.body: Brush-turkeys live in rainforest and wet forest, and also in drier scrubs [ref:am-brushturkey]. In the Hann country the thick cover is patchy: Rinyirru's closed forests and vine thickets 'are very restricted' and occur 'on lighter textured soils with a permanent watertable, on levee banks subject to seasonal flooding, in fire-protected areas' [ref:qpws-rinyirru-2013], and 'gallery rainforest grows along parts of the Normanby and Kennedy rivers' [ref:qpws-rinyirru-culture]. That is where to expect the mounds, not on the open grassy woodland.

sections.heading: Fire and the scrub
sections.body: High-intensity fires have burnt into the edges of Rinyirru's vine thickets, and park management uses 'low intensity perimeter burns to protect margins of vine thickets' [ref:qpws-rinyirru-2013]: the turkeys' cover depends on keeping hot fires out.

sections.heading: On country today
sections.body: The upper Hann is the Possum People's country and the middle and lower Hann are Thaypan country, under native title determinations of November 2023 [ref:fca-possum] [ref:fca-thaypan]; Rinyirru is jointly managed by the Rinyirru Aboriginal Corporation and the Queensland Government [ref:qpws-rinyirru-culture]. Native title holders may hunt and gather for personal, domestic and non-commercial communal needs without the licences others need [ref:nta1993]. The brush-turkey is a protected native animal [ref:qld-nca]; everyone else leaves the birds and their mounds alone.

locations.summary: Brush-turkeys are mainly a rainforest bird, but the Atlas of Living Australia holds records from the Mitchell River country west of Mt Carbine [ref:am-brushturkey] [ref:ala].

sections.heading: Where it lives here
sections.body: Brush-turkeys are mainly a rainforest bird, but they also live in drier scrubs [ref:am-brushturkey]. The Atlas of Living Australia holds records from the Mitchell River country west of Mt Carbine [ref:ala]. Look for them in the thicker, shadier scrub along the rivers and gullies rather than in the open grassy woodland.

sections.heading: On country today
sections.body: The Western Yalanji determinations (2013) recognise rights to hunt and gather for personal, domestic and non-commercial communal purposes [ref:brady2013].

locations.summary: Diwan is a bird of the Eastern Kuku Yalanji rainforest. The Queensland Parks and Wildlife Service records the same knowledge: when blue ginger is fruiting, it is time to catch diwan [ref:qpws-daintree]. In Daintree National Park brush-turkeys are seen all year round [ref:qpws-daintree].

sections.heading: Seasons here
sections.body: The Queensland Parks and Wildlife Service puts it the same way: when blue ginger is fruiting, it is time to catch diwan [ref:qpws-daintree].

sections.heading: On country today
sections.body: Much of the turkey's rainforest is now Eastern Kuku Yalanji land. In 2021 the Daintree, Ngalba Bulal, Kalkajaka and Hope Islands national parks were handed back, to be jointly managed with the Queensland Government until Traditional Owners take over sole management [ref:handback2021]. The Eastern Kuku Yalanji native title determination (2007) recognises rights to hunt animals and gather, but not for trade or commerce [ref:walker2007]. The right to give permission to come onto country belongs to the Traditional Owners [ref:walker2007].
